newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: VA Tech seen reporting strong H1 profit.
newsitem.headline: VA Tech seen reporting strong H1 profit.

text.p: A healthy rise in new orders, outweighing an increased tax burden, should help Austrian engineering group VA Technologie to post a strong first half result on Wednesday, analysts said on Monday.

"The results should be very good. Order books have further improved, the group is planning a restructuring which will make it more efficient, so we should see a strong performance in the second half," said Gerhard Auer, analyst at ICE Securities in London.

Die Erste analyst Horst Simbuerger said he expected first-half turnover at 10.25 billion schilling, compared with 9.3 billion in 1995, and pre-tax earnings at 370 million schilling against 322 million last year.
VA Technologie indicated last month it expected a double digit increase in pre-tax profits in the first six months due to a record number of new orders.

But analysts agree VA Technologie will like other Austrian firms in the sector feel a squeeze in net profits as a result of the government's scrapping of tax credits on losses carried forward in 1996 and 1997.

Alan Coats, steel analyst at Merrill Lynch predicted the tax changes would take a relatively heavy toll on VA Technologie. He saw earnings per share falling to 70.4 schillings from 78.8 for the full year and net profit down to 1.11 billion schilling from 1.34 billion in 1995.

Die Erste's Simbuerger predicted a modest rise in net profit to 300 million schillings from 294 million a year ago, with earnings per share at 70 and 76 schillings respectively for 1996 and 1997. Die Erste has retained its "buy" for the company's shares.
While the tax changes would put a number of Austrian companies in the doldrums, the long-term outlook for VA Tech remained rosy, ICE Securities' Auer said.

"As the group is world leading in a number of products on the metallurgical and energy engineering side, one would assume earnings will increase significantly in the long term and on that basis the company should outperform the market," he said.
